title: Right Mindfulness at the Time of Death
author: Zhanran
excerpt: The principle of rebirth: right mindfulness at the time of death evokes the Buddha's coming to welcome one.

inline.s: The principle of rebirth: right mindfulness at the time of death evokes the Buddha's coming to welcome one.

Q: Why must one have right mindfulness at the time of death in order to be reborn? Amitābha Buddha's five kalpas of contemplation and his cultivation through countless kalpas — his entire great vow — are meant to save every sentient being. With such great compassion, could he fail to exert his awe-inspiring power and vow to receive us when our death comes?
[Right mindfulness] The thought of reciting the Buddha's name, unmingled with delusive thoughts.
A:

At the death of every sentient being, Amitābha Buddha is there to receive them. It is only that beings without right mindfulness at death cannot see him, and so they follow their own delusive thoughts and receive rebirth according to their karma.
Therefore, one must have right mindfulness at death in order to see Amitābha Buddha come to receive one, and to follow the Buddha to rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss.

[It is only that beings without right mindfulness at death cannot see him, and so they follow their own delusive thoughts and receive rebirth according to their karma.] Therefore Master Shandao, in his
Essay on Right Mindfulness for Rebirth at Death
says:
“If a single thought goes astray
(if the single thought at death is not right mindfulness but a delusive thought)
one suffers for kalpas on end
(one will undergo suffering through many kalpas of transmigration in the six realms)
On this principle, Master Zhongfeng, honored as the Ancient Buddha of Jiangnan, taught in his Three Sessions of Recitation:
“Yet although it is said that Amitābha gathers sentient beings in for rebirth, one must believe
that it is solely the mind's own manifestation
the intertwining of stimulus and response
, and in the end
(after all)
is not obtained from outside

[Solely the mind's own manifestation] Amitābha Buddha comes to receive (to gather in) sentient beings, and this is solely the mind's own manifestation; it is so because of the intertwining of stimulus and response, not because it is obtained from outside. Therefore only one who has right mindfulness at death can see the Buddha come, while other people around cannot see him. As for dying beings who lack right mindfulness at death, because their own minds are turbid and confused and they have no sense of right mindfulness (ten uninterrupted thoughts), naturally Amitābha Buddha's coming to receive them will not manifest within their minds either, and so they cannot see the Buddha come,
and it is not that Amitābha Buddha does not come to receive them
Therefore whether one attains rebirth depends entirely on whether one has right mindfulness at death
(ten uninterrupted thoughts at death)
This is why
Master Shandao, an emanation of Amitābha Buddha, and Master Yongming, also an emanation of Amitābha Buddha, both earnestly taught:
one must accomplish ten uninterrupted thoughts at death
(see
The Conditions for Rebirth
. These are the teachings of Amitābha Buddha himself!

[The intertwining of stimulus and response] The stimulus of sentient beings and the response of Amitābha Buddha meet and interpenetrate. As for the principle of this intertwining of stimulus and response at death, Master Yinguang, an emanation of Mahasthamaprapta, taught in his Preface to A Beginner's Guide to Pure Land Practice:

“The minds of sentient beings are like water, and Amitābha Buddha is like the moon. When sentient beings' faith and vows are complete and they sincerely evoke the Buddha, the Buddha responds, just as the moon appears when the water is clear. If the mind is not pure and not sincere, but accords with greed, hatred, and delusion and turns its back on the Buddha, then it is like turbid, agitated water: though the moon never fails to shine upon it, it cannot be clearly reflected.”

Translation: The minds of sentient beings are like water, and Amitābha Buddha is like the moon. When sentient beings' faith and vows are complete and they sincerely evoke the Buddha, the Buddha responds, just as the moon appears when the water is clear and still (a metaphor for how the pure mind of right mindfulness evokes Amitābha Buddha's reception). If the mind is not pure and not sincere, but accords with greed, hatred, and delusion and opposes the Buddha, then it is like turbid, agitated water: though the Buddha-moon shines upon it without omission (a metaphor for how Amitābha Buddha is always receiving every dying sentient being), it cannot be clearly reflected (a metaphor for how an agitated, turbid, scattered mind cannot evoke Amitābha Buddha's reception,
but instead follows its own delusive thoughts and receives rebirth according to karma

“Only when the water is clear and still does it appear; when the water is turbid and agitated it is hidden. The moon certainly makes no choice or rejection; the reason it does not appear is that the water is murky, turbid, and churning, so there is no way for it to receive the moon's reflection.”

Translation: Only when the water is clear and still does the moon's reflection appear; when the water is turbid and agitated, the moon's reflection does not appear. The moon certainly shines without choice or rejection; the reason it does not appear is that the water is murky, turbid, and churning, so the moon's reflection cannot be revealed. (Metaphor: only those sentient beings with right mindfulness at death can see Amitābha Buddha's reception, while those without right mindfulness at death cannot see it. Amitābha Buddha certainly receives every dying sentient being without choice or rejection, and the reason those without right mindfulness at death cannot see his reception is that
their own minds are murky and turbid
and scattered,
and so
they follow their own delusive thoughts and receive rebirth according to karma

Therefore, for one who recites the Buddha's name, single-minded right mindfulness at death is of the utmost importance. The thousands upon thousands of recitations, and even reciting all day and all year, are nothing but the ripening of this one thought of Buddha-recitation,
so as to ensure that at the time of death this thought continues uninterrupted and evokes Amitābha Buddha's reception
. Therefore Master Shandao, an emanation of Amitābha Buddha, taught:

“Because calling the name is easy, one is reborn through continuity. If one can continue thought after thought, taking life's end as the term, then ten out of ten are reborn, a hundred out of a hundred are reborn.”
(see
Master Shandao's Pure Land Teaching
) Master Lianchi taught:
“Now that one is single-mindedly undefiled, then
(at the approach of death)
within, right mindfulness congeals; without, the Buddha's welcome is evoked; casting off this karmic body, one is reborn in that land.”
(Commentary on the Amitābha Sutra)
[Continuity] The thoughts of Buddha-recitation succeed one another, uninterrupted by delusive thoughts.
Q: The Sutra Spoken by the Buddha in Praise of the Pure Land and the Buddha's Reception says:

“If for one day and night, or two, or three, or four, or five, or six, or seven, one keeps the thought in mind without confusion — when that good man or good woman is about to die, Measureless Life Buddha, together with his immeasurable shravaka disciples and host of bodhisattvas, surrounds him before and behind, comes and stands before him,
and with compassion empowers and protects him, causing his mind to be undefiled
. Once he has cast off his life, he follows the Buddha's assembly and is born in the pure Buddha-land of the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Measureless Life.”

Since one has already attained keeping the thought in mind without confusion (single-mindedness), why is it also said that after Amitābha Buddha comes he “with compassion empowers and protects him, causing his mind to be undefiled”?

A: Keeping the thought in mind without confusion (single-mindedness) is what evokes the Buddha's welcome, but keeping the thought in mind without confusion is a shallow level of practice, and it is often not enough to keep the mind undefiled when the four elements dissolve and suffering presses and demons appear; therefore Amitābha Buddha “with compassion empowers and protects him, causing his mind to be undefiled,” so as to ensure rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss.
The Sutra on Praising the Merits of the Buddhas says:
“When his life is about to end, he believes and rejoices with one mind, and his mindfulness is not forgotten or abandoned
this is right mindfulness at death, which evokes the Buddha's welcome
Amitābha Buddha will
(lead)
the host of monks
(the shravaka disciples and the assembly of bodhisattvas)
to stand before that person, and the demons can never destroy such
(this good man's or good woman's)
mind of right awakening.”
Here, “the demons can never destroy such a mind of right awakening” is precisely because Amitābha Buddha “with compassion empowers and protects him, causing his mind to be undefiled.”
The patriarchs' teachings on right mindfulness at death are now transcribed with annotations as follows:
Master Shandao was an emanation of Amitābha Buddha. Therefore what Master Shandao said is equivalent to what Amitābha Buddha himself proclaimed. Master Shandao's
Essay on Right Mindfulness for Rebirth at Death
says:
“If, when the illness is grave and death approaches, relatives must not shed tears and weep, nor utter sounds of sighing and grief, confusing the sick person's mind and spirit
and causing him to lose right mindfulness

. Rather, they should recite the Buddha's name aloud together, and only after the breath has ceased may they wail and weep. The moment there is the slightest attachment to the world, it becomes a hindrance and one cannot be liberated. If one can have someone who understands the Pure Land come frequently to encourage him, that is extremely fortunate. If one acts accordingly, one will certainly be reborn in transcendence — of this there is no doubt.”

If, when the illness is grave and death approaches, the relatives must not shed tears and weep, nor utter sounds of sighing and grief, lest the sick person's mind and spirit be confused and he lose right mindfulness. Rather, they must recite the Buddha's name in unison, and only after the sick person's breath has ceased may they wail and weep. For the moment the sick person has the slightest attachment to the world, it becomes a hindrance to rebirth and he cannot be liberated. If one can have someone who understands the Pure Land come frequently to encourage him, this is most fortunate. If one acts accordingly, the sick person will certainly be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss, beyond all doubt.
[Master Shandao was an emanation of Amitābha Buddha] Master Yinguang, an emanation of Mahasthamaprapta, praised Master Shandao:

“He accorded with principle and with capacities, and skillfully taught the essentials of the Dharma. That he was a transformation body of Amitābha is hardly an idle tradition. The Second Patriarch of the Lotus school is revered for ten thousand generations.”
(Preface to the Re-carved Shandao Commentary on the Contemplation Sutra of Immeasurable Life Buddha)

Whether cleric or layperson, or one who has never recited the Buddha's name, whoever uses this method will be reborn — of this there is no doubt. I have often seen people who in ordinary times recite the Buddha's name, bow, and praise, and vow to be reborn in the West, with great earnestness
(sincerity and zeal)

. Yet when illness comes, they fear death and say nothing at all about rebirth and liberation. Only when breath has ceased and life is over, and consciousness has fallen into the dark realm, do they begin to recite the Buddha's name and ring the bell. This is like shutting the gate after the thief has gone — what use is it? The matter of birth and death is grave,
and one must apply one's own effort to succeed
If a single thought goes astray
(if the single thought at death is not right mindfulness but a delusive thought)
, one suffers for kalpas on end
, who will take one's place?
Think on this! Think on this!
When there is nothing the matter, one should take up this method diligently and uphold it; this is the great matter of the time of death.”

This method of “right mindfulness for rebirth at death” (the sick person must strive to maintain right mindfulness at death; relatives must not weep and wail, lest they disturb the sick person's right mindfulness at death; and a good teacher's constant guidance and encouragement can help the sick person raise up and maintain right mindfulness at death) — whether cleric or layperson, or one who has never recited the Buddha's name, whoever uses it will be reborn, beyond all doubt. I have seen many people in the world who in ordinary times recite the Buddha's name, bow, and praise, and vow to be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss with great sincerity and zeal. Yet when illness comes, they fear death and say nothing at all about rebirth and liberation. Only when their own breath has ceased and life is over, and their consciousness has fallen into the dark realm, do they come to recite the Buddha's name and ring the bell. This is like shutting the gate after the thief has gone (the thief has already carried the goods away, and only then does one shut the gate to guard against theft) — what use is it? The matter of birth and death is grave,
and one must diligently apply one's own effort
If the single thought at death goes astray
(if the single thought at death is not right mindfulness but a delusive thought)
, the consequence is suffering for kalpas on end
, who will take one's place?
You must consider this well! Consider it well!

Before illness has yet come, one should diligently take up and uphold this method of “right mindfulness for rebirth at death” (one must make full preparation for right mindfulness at death — this is what Master Yongming called “preparing the ford and bridge in advance” — and one should also warn one's relatives that they must not weep and wail at that time; it would be even better to have the help of a good teacher at death). This is the great matter of the time of death!

Master Yongming was an emanation of Amitābha Buddha. Therefore what Master Yongming said is equivalent to what Amitābha Buddha himself proclaimed. Master Yongming's Collection on the Common Return of the Ten Thousand Good Deeds says:
“When walking the path
(circumambulating)

and bowing in reverence, when reciting the Buddha's name and making vows, one should be sorrowful, urgent, and sincere, with no other thoughts — as if going to execution, as if in prison, pursued by hateful thieves, pressed by water and fire — seeking help with one mind, vowing to escape the wheel of suffering, quickly realizing the non-arising, and widely saving sentient beings, perpetuating the Three Jewels, and vowing to repay the four kindnesses. Such sincere resolve will certainly not be cast away in vain.”
When circumambulating and bowing in reverence, when reciting the Buddha's name and making vows,
one must be sorrowful, urgent, and sincere
with no other miscellaneous thoughts
, as if
at the execution ground, as if in prison, as if
pursued by hateful thieves,
as if
water and fire
were pressing in
, seeking help with one mind, vowing to escape
suffering
, quickly realizing the non-arising, and widely saving
sentient beings

, perpetuating (inheriting and carrying forward) the Three Jewels (the Buddha Jewel, the Dharma Jewel, and the Sangha Jewel) and vowing to repay the four kindnesses (the kindness of parents, of sentient beings, of the country, and of the Three Jewels)
If
this
resolve
is sincere
one will certainly be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss (one will certainly not be cast away in vain)

[Master Yongming, an emanation of Amitābha Buddha] Master Yongming was an emanation of Amitābha Buddha, and so the seventeenth day of the eleventh lunar month, his birthday, has been taken as Amitābha Buddha's anniversary. Of Master Yongming, Master Yinguang, an emanation of Mahasthamaprapta, praised him saying:
“Master Yongming was a transformation body of Amitābha Buddha. Greatly compassionate and greatly merciful, he opened and transformed sentient beings.”
(The Collected Writings of Master Yinguang
World Buddhist Laymen's Grove, Recorded Dharma Talks)
[Those with consciousness]
those who possess mind-consciousness,
that is, sentient beings of the six realms.
[Bi (
bi
) prison]
A jail.

“If one's words do not match one's deeds, and the power of one's faith is slight, with no mind of thought-after-thought continuity but rather an intention of repeated interruption, relying on such negligence and hoping for rebirth at the end of life — such a one will be veiled by karmic obstacles, and I fear he will hardly meet a good friend; when wind and fire press upon him, right mindfulness will not be accomplished.”

If one's words and deeds do not match, and the power of one's faith is slight, with no mind of thought-after-thought continuity but rather an intention of repeated interruption (the thoughts of Buddha-recitation interrupted by delusive thoughts), and one relies on such negligent practice, then though at the end of life one hopes for rebirth in the Pure Land, one will be blocked by karmic obstacles; and I fear it will be hard to meet a good spiritual guide who can enable one to accomplish right mindfulness at death. When the four elements of the body (earth, water, fire, and wind) dissolve and wind and fire press upon one, one will be unable to accomplish right mindfulness at death, and so will not attain rebirth.

[Words and deeds not matching] One's words and deeds do not accord. Verbally one claims true faith and earnest vows, but in actual practice one's faith is not true and one's vows are not earnest: one fears hardship and suffering, is lazy and negligent. Therefore Master Yongming's next line is:
“The power of faith is slight.”
And he rebuked them further:
Relying on this negligence.”
One who recites the Buddha's name should keep firmly in mind the Buddha's earnest teaching in the Sutra of Measureless Life Buddha:
Though for one lifetime one toils and suffers
, in a moment afterward one is born in the Land of Measureless Life,
with boundless happiness
“Why is that? The present is the cause, and the time of death is the fruit; the cause must be true, and then the fruit will not be false. If one wishes
to accomplish the ten thoughts at death
, one need only prepare the ford and bridge in advance, gather merit, and dedicate it to that time
(dedicate it to the moment of death)
, so that not one thought is lacking
(achieving thought-after-thought continuity)
, and then there is nothing to worry about.”

Why is that? Cultivation now is the cause, and whether one is reborn at the end of life is the fruit; the cause must be true, and then the fruit will not be false. If one wishes to accomplish the ten thoughts at death, one must make preparations in advance (accumulating thought-after-thought continuity until it becomes second nature), gather merit, and dedicate it to the moment of death, achieving thought-after-thought continuity; then one will certainly be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss (and there is nothing to worry about).
[Accomplishing the ten thoughts at death] Accomplishing ten uninterrupted thoughts at death. (
see
The Conditions for Rebirth
) [Preparing the ford and bridge] “Ford and bridge” means a ferry crossing and a bridge. “Preparing the ford and bridge in advance” means making preparations beforehand.
Master Lianchi's Commentary on the Amitābha Sutra says:

“Those who are confused at the end of life are so because in ordinary times they follow delusive thoughts, do not cultivate right mindfulness, and their minds are mostly scattered. When the warmth of the body is about to be relinquished, all that they have done in their lives appears before them, and their minds and spirits are terrified, their movements and pauses wild and flustered. Those who should enter hell see mountains of knives and forests of swords as pleasure gardens. Those who should fall among animals take the womb of a horse or the belly of a donkey as a splendid hall. Even those who have done good and should be born as humans or gods cannot avoid feeling love and hatred toward their parents. Even the small saints of initial resolve cannot correctly know their entering and departing. All of this is what is called confusion. Riding on this confusion, they receive rebirth according to karma within the three realms and seven destinies. Now, since one is single-mindedly undefiled,
within, right mindfulness congeals; without, the Buddha's welcome is evoked

, and casting off this karmic body, one is born in that land. As the Buddha said, “When the mind is pure, the Buddha-land is pure,” and again, “All Buddha-lands are upheld by thought alone.” When the pure contemplation is accomplished, one will certainly attain rebirth — of this there is no doubt.”

Those who are confused at the end of life are all so because in ordinary times they follow delusive thoughts, do not cultivate right mindfulness, and their minds are mostly scattered. When the four elements dissolve, all that they have done in their lives appears before them, and their minds and spirits are terrified and their bearing loses all composure. Those who should enter hell see mountains of knives and forests of swords as beautiful gardens. Those who should fall among animals take the womb of a horse or the belly of a donkey for a magnificent hall. Even those who have done good and should be born in the human or heavenly realm cannot avoid, at the moment of entering the womb, loving the mother and hating the father and so taking a male body, or loving the father and hating the mother and so taking a female body. Even the small saints of the first fruit and bodhisattvas of initial resolve still have the delusion of the intervening skandha and cannot correctly know their entering and departing from the womb. All of this is confusion. Because of this confusion at the end of life, they receive rebirth according to karma within the seven destinies of the three realms. Now that one has accomplished single-mindedness in reciting the Buddha's name, then at the end of life, within, right mindfulness congeals, and without, the Buddha's welcome is evoked; casting off this karmic body, one goes directly to rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss. Just as the Buddha said: ‘When the mind is pure, the Buddha-land is pure.’ (When one's mind is pure, the Buddha-land in which one is born is also pure.) The Buddha also said: ‘All Buddha-lands are upheld by thought alone.’ (All Buddha-lands are entirely upheld by the mind's thought.) Therefore, when one who recites the Buddha's name accomplishes the pure contemplation, one will certainly attain rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss. Of this, of course, there is not the slightest doubt.

[The seven destinies] Hell, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, immortals, gods, and asuras. “Destiny” means the direction toward which one tends. [Buddha-land] The territory taught and transformed by one Buddha; there are distinctions of pure land, defiled land, reward land, and dharma-nature land.
Master Ouyi's Essential Explanation of the Buddha-Spoken Amitābha Sutra says:

“Q: Does reciting the name with a scattered mind also remove offenses? A: The merit of the name is inconceivable — how could it fail to remove offenses? But it does not ensure rebirth, because leisurely, scattered goodness is hard pressed to match the offenses accumulated since beginningless time. You should know that if the accumulated offenses had substance and form, the entire realm of empty space could not contain them; though for a hundred years, day and night, one recite Amitābha a hundred thousand times, and each utterance erases offenses of eighty billion kalpas of birth and death, still the offenses erased are like soil on the fingernail, while the offenses not erased are like the soil of the great earth. Only when one recites to the point of single-mindedness is it like a strong man breaking out through a siege, no longer to be held back by the three armies.”

Q: Does reciting the Buddha's name with a scattered mind also remove offenses? A: The merit of the name is inconceivable — how could it fail to remove offenses? But it does not necessarily lead to rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss. This is because leisurely, scattered goodness is hard pressed to match the offenses accumulated since beginningless time. One should know that if the offenses accumulated since beginningless time had substance and form, the entire realm of empty space could not contain them; though in a hundred years one recites Amitābha a hundred thousand times each day and night, and each utterance erases eighty billion kalpas of grave offenses of birth and death, still the offenses erased are like soil on the fingernail, while the offenses not erased are like the soil of the ten directions' great earth. Only when one recites to the point of single-mindedness is it like a warrior breaking out through a siege, and the three armies of the foe (that is, afflictions and karmic obstacles) can do nothing to him.

Here Master Ouyi clearly points out that reciting the Buddha's name with a scattered mind is not incapable of removing offenses, but does not necessarily lead to rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, and he explains the principle: “You should know that if the accumulated offenses had substance and form, the entire realm of empty space could not contain them; though for a hundred years, day and night, one recite Amitābha a hundred thousand times, and each utterance erases offenses of eighty billion kalpas of birth and death, still the offenses erased are like soil on the fingernail, while the offenses not erased are like the soil of the great earth.” Then what should one do? Master Ouyi continues: “Only when one recites to the point of single-mindedness is it like a strong man breaking out through a siege, no longer to be held back by the three armies.” Therefore the way out is “only reciting to the point of single-mindedness.” This is why the World-Honored One clearly taught that one should recite the Buddha's name single-mindedly, and repeatedly urged one to “practice as taught.”

[Soil on the fingernail] Also written “soil on the nail”; soil on a fingernail. In the scriptures and treatises, soil on the fingernail is often compared with the soil of the great earth as a simile, describing the former as extremely small and the latter as extremely abundant.

“Q: Do the ten thoughts of the Great Text and the one thought of the King of Jewels refer to ordinary times or to the time of death? A: The ten thoughts apply to both times. The ten thoughts of the morning session belong to ordinary times; the ten thoughts that bring rebirth are the same as the ten thoughts of calling the name in the Contemplation Sutra, and belong to the time of death. The one thought refers only to the time of death.”

A student asked: The Sutra of Measureless Life speaks of “attaining rebirth through ten thoughts,” and the Treatise on the King of Jewels of Buddha-Recitation Samādhi speaks of “attaining rebirth through one thought” — do these ten thoughts and one thought refer to ordinary times or to the time of death? Master Ouyi answered: The commonly spoken “ten thoughts” have two cases, one referring to ordinary times and one to the time of death. The “ten thoughts of the morning session” advocated by Chan Master Ciyun refers to ordinary times; “attaining rebirth through ten thoughts” is the same as “calling the name ten times” in the Contemplation Sutra of Immeasurable Life, and both refer to the final ten thoughts at the time of death. As for “attaining rebirth through one thought” spoken of in the Treatise on the King of Jewels, it refers only to the final thought at the time of death.

[The ten thoughts of the Great Text] Refers to “attaining rebirth through ten thoughts” as taught in the Sutra of Measureless Life. [The one thought of the King of Jewels] Refers to “attaining rebirth through one thought” as taught in the Treatise on the King of Jewels of Buddha-Recitation Samādhi, Chapter Nine, “The Gate of One Thought and Ten Thoughts in This Life and the Next.”

“Q: If both ten thoughts and one thought bring rebirth, why are seven days needed? A: Without the seven days' practice of ordinary times, how could there be the ten thoughts or one thought at death? Even the evil and perverse person of the lowest of the low grades has matured former causes, and so is able to meet a good friend at death and, upon hearing, believe and vow. Such a thing is one in ten thousand — how could one count on luck? The Questions on the Pure Land refutes this in the greatest detail; people today must read it.”

The student asked again: If the ten thoughts or one thought at death can both lead to rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss, why is the practice of single-minded Buddha-recitation still necessary? Master Ouyi answered: Without the practice of single-mindedness in ordinary times, where would the ten thoughts or one thought at death come from? Even the evil and perverse person of the lowest of the low grades has matured former causes, and so is able to meet a good friend at death and, upon hearing, believe and vow. Such a thing is one in ten thousand — how could one count on luck! The Questions on the Pure Land refutes this fallacy of “ten thoughts or one thought both bring rebirth, so why need single-mindedness in ordinary times?” in the greatest detail; people today must read it.

On the question of the ten thoughts at death, Master Ouyi discusses in the Discourse on the Peak of the Spirit, “Preface to the Pure Land Repentance and the Society for Releasing Life”: the ten thoughts at death require deeply planting good roots before right mindfulness can appear at death. If at present, as soon as adverse or favorable conditions arise, one no longer has right mindfulness, how much less will one be able to maintain right mindfulness at the time of death? Moreover, now, under clear skies and bright sun, when all is plain and bright, one still cannot believe, accept, and practice the true admonitions and teachings of a clear teacher and good friend — and yet one vainly hopes that when suffering appears at death, one need only rely on a good friend's reminder and teaching to believe, accept, and practice? What is more, at the time of death, how can one be sure that a true good friend will appear? And even if a true good friend does appear, if at the time of his instruction the person's consciousness is dim and confused, to seek his faith and understanding would be utterly impossible! (The original text reads: “Now, the ten thoughts at death require deeply planting good roots. If at present, as soon as adverse or favorable conditions arise, one no longer has right mindfulness, how much less at death? Moreover, when suffering appears at death, one can only rely on a good friend's reminder; yet now, under clear skies and bright sun, one still cannot believe, accept, and practice the true maxims of a clear teacher and good friend! When death comes, who can guarantee that a good friend will appear? Suppose one appears and gives instruction, but the consciousness is dim and confused — to seek faith and understanding from such a one is again a thing that absolutely cannot be obtained.”)

From this we know that attaining rebirth through ten thoughts means the final ten thoughts at death, and attaining rebirth through one thought means the final thought at death; the final decision at death is the true decision. At the time of death it is like a person arriving at an airport: ordinarily he says he will go here and there, but where he actually goes depends entirely on which plane he finally boards. Therefore, being able at the very end to recite one or ten Buddha-names with single-minded concentration is extremely crucial.

As to the relationship between attaining rebirth through ten thoughts or one thought and single-mindedness, Master Ouyi clearly states: “Without the seven days' practice of ordinary times (the practice of single-mindedness in ordinary times), how could there be the ten thoughts or one thought at death?”

As to the state of Buddha-recitation of the person of the five perverse deeds and ten evils who attains rebirth through ten thoughts at death, Master Yinguang taught: though he has not personally realized single-mindedness, at the time of death his mind has, after all, no thought other than the thought of Buddha-recitation. (Master Yinguang's original words: “In the Contemplation Sutra, the five perverse deeds and ten evils, when about to die, see the marks of hell appear. A good friend (original note: whether monk or lay, man or woman, whoever can teach him to recite the Buddha's name is called a good friend) teaches him to recite the Buddha's name, whether ten utterances or fewer than ten; when his life ends straightway, he also attains rebirth with his karma carried along by the Buddha's compassionate power. These ten thoughts, compared with ordinary ten thoughts, are as different in intensity as heaven from an abyss, and so he attains rebirth. Pressed by the extreme suffering of hell, as soon as he hears the Buddha's name he recites it with his whole spirit. Apart from this thought, he has absolutely no other thought. Though he has not personally realized single-mindedness, his mind has, after all, no other thought.” (The Collected Writings of Master Yinguang, Third Series, Volume Two, “Reply to Layman Chen Xinru”))
Master Xing'an's Disquisition on Buddha-Recitation and Demon-Possession says:

“If the single thought at death is confused, not only will one fail to be reborn in the nine grades, but one will hardly escape the three evil paths; though the Buddha is greatly compassionate, he cannot save me. What is to be done! What is to be done!”

If the single thought at death is confused, not only will one fail to attain rebirth in the nine grades in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss, but one will hardly escape falling into the three evil paths (hell, hungry ghosts, and animals); though Amitābha Buddha is greatly compassionate and merciful, he cannot save me either. What is to be done! What is to be done!

[The three paths] Also written “the three destinies.” That is, the fire path, the knife path, and the blood path; their meaning is the same as hell, hungry ghosts, and animals of the three evil paths, being places drawn forth by the various evil karmas of body, speech, and mind. 1. The fire path: that is, the hell realm, where sentient beings constantly suffer from boiling cauldrons and burning coals, and where there are many fires, hence “fire path.” 2. The knife path: that is, the hungry ghost realm, where sentient beings constantly endure the suffering of being driven and pressed by knives and staves, hence “knife path.” 3. The blood path: that is, the animal realm, where the strong overpower the weak and devour one another, drinking blood and eating flesh, hence “blood path.”
Master Chewu's Posthumous Collection says:

“The single thought before us now is arisen from conditions and has no nature; being without nature, it arises from conditions. If it does not arise in the Buddha realm, it arises in the nine realms. If we consider that, being arisen from conditions, it has no nature, then Buddha and sentient beings are equally one emptiness. If we consider that, being without nature, it arises from conditions, then the ten realms are vastly different in superiority and inferiority. King Ajatashatru, at the time of death, had a fly brushed from his face by the fly-whisk bearer; with a single thought of anger he fell to become a poisonous snake. A woman crossing a river let go with her hand, and her child fell into the water; because she tried to rescue the child, she drowned with him, and by the power of that compassionate mind she was born in heaven. Now, a single thought of compassion or of anger thus divides heaven from animal — how then can this condition-arisen single thought at the time of death be taken lightly? If one takes this mind and turns it to mindfulness of Amitābha and seeks rebirth in the Pure Land, will one not see the Buddha and attain rebirth?”

Our present single thought is dependent-arising yet without self-nature, and without self-nature yet dependent-arising. If it is not born into the Buddha-realm, then it is born into the nine realms. Seen from the standpoint of dependent-arising yet without self-nature, sentient beings and Buddhas are equal, all being one emptiness. Seen from the standpoint of without self-nature yet dependent-arising, among the ten realms the superior and inferior differ very greatly. When King Aqida was at the point of death, because the fly-whisker was careless and fanned his face, a single thought of anger arose; and because this final thought at death was one of anger, he fell and became a venomous snake. A woman crossing a river lost her footing, and her child fell into the water; because she strove to save the child, she and the child were both drowned. And because her final thought at death was one of compassion, this woman was reborn in heaven. When the final thought at death is compassion or anger, the compassionate are born in heaven and the angry are born among animals, and so the superior and inferior part. Can we be careless about that single thought of dependent-arising at the moment of death? If, at that moment of death, one fixes this mind in mindfulness on Amitābha Buddha and seeks rebirth in the Pure Land, how could one fail to see the Buddha and be reborn?

[Without self-nature]“All dharmas are without self-nature” means that all dharmas have no real substance, being all illusory appearances, like things in a dream. Without self-nature is also called natureless. The Treatise on Consciousness-Only says: “All dharmas are without self-nature.” The Lotus Sutra says: “Know that all dharmas are constantly without nature.” The Surangama Sutra says: “All illusions become natureless.” [King Aqida]That is, King Aqida, who throughout his life built countless stupas, made offerings to the Triple Gem, protected the right Dharma, and had vast merit. At the moment of death, because an attendant’s hand slipped and fanned his face with a fan, anger arose, and he fell and became a venomous snake. The matter is seen in the Miscellaneous Parable Sutra.
[The single thought of dependent-arising at the moment of death]That thought at the moment of death that decides where the consciousness is reborn.

[But this single thought cannot be achieved by chance. One must preserve it with sincerity and hold it with constancy. Therefore, when we recite this one phrase of Amitābha, a thousand thoughts and ten thousand thoughts, even to reciting throughout the whole day and the whole year, is nothing other than to make this single thought familiar. If indeed this single thought becomes perfectly familiar, then at the moment of death there is only this one thought, with no other thought. The Great Master Zhizhe said: ‘The mind fixed in samādhi at the moment of death is the mind that receives rebirth in the Pure Land.’ Now to have only this one thought and no other — is this not the mind fixed in samādhi? If the thought is truly like this, then if one does not see Amitābha, whom else would one see? If one is not reborn in the Pure Land, where else would one be reborn? I only fear that we do not have sufficient confidence in ourselves.]

But this final thought at death cannot be achieved by chance. One must preserve it with sincerity and hold it with constancy. Therefore, with regard to this one phrase of Amitābha, our thousand thoughts and ten thousand thoughts, even to reciting throughout the whole day and the whole year, is nothing other than to make this thought of Buddha-recitation familiar, so as to ensure that the thought at the moment of death is mindfulness of Amitābha. If indeed the single thought of Buddha-recitation becomes perfectly familiar, then at the moment of death there is only this thought of Buddha-recitation and no other thought. The Great Master Zhizhe said: ‘The mind fixed in samādhi at the moment of death is the mind that receives rebirth in the Pure Land.’ Now to have only the thought of Buddha-recitation and no other thought — is this not the mind fixed in samādhi? Since at death it is the mind in samādhi, if one does not see Amitābha Buddha, whom else would one see? If one is not reborn in the Pure Land, where else would one be reborn? I only fear that we ourselves have not truly believed in the principle stated above. If we truly believed, how could we fail to strive to make this thought of Buddha-recitation familiar and be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss?

[Making this single thought familiar]This means to achieve what the Mahasthamaprapta spoke of, the “unbroken pure thought,” which is what the Great Master Shandao (the second patriarch of the Pure Land school) called “thought after thought continuing without break.” (Please note: “thought after thought continuing without break” means that the thought of Buddha-recitation, thought after thought, continues without break, and is not that situation of the mouth continuously reciting the Buddha while the mind is given over to deluded thought.) The Great Master Shandao said: ‘Therefore the Great Sage (Śākyamuni Buddha), with compassionate pity, directly urges us to single-mindedly call upon the Name; precisely because calling upon the Name is easy, continuous [recitation] brings rebirth. If one can practice thought after thought continuing without break, taking the end of one’s life as the limit, then of ten, ten are reborn; of a hundred, a hundred are reborn. … I wish that all people would think this over well: whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, one must sharpen the mind and discipline oneself, forgoing it neither by day nor by night; when the previous thought ends, the next thought immediately arises, forever enjoying the Dharma-joy of the unconditioned, and even to the attainment of Buddhahood — how joyful it would be!’ (See
Master Shandao’s Pure Land Teaching

) Therefore, that everyday thought after thought continuing without break is the safeguard for right mindfulness at the moment of death being clear; and that clear right mindfulness at the moment of death is in turn the key to rebirth in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.

blocks.text: The Instruction of the Great Master Yinguang

inline.s: The Collected Writings of Master Yinguang, Third Compilation
Volume Two
Letter in Reply to the Layman Chen Xinru says:
[In the Contemplation Sutra, a person of the five heinous offenses and the ten evil deeds, about to come to the end of life, sees the signs of hell appear. There is a good spiritual friend
(original note: this is without regard to monk or layman, male or female; whoever can teach him to recite the Buddha is called a good spiritual friend)

who teaches him to recite the Buddha, and if only ten recitations, or even fewer than ten, then straightway he comes to the end of life and is still able to rely on the Buddha’s compassionate power and be reborn carrying his karma. These ten recitations, compared with ordinary ten recitations, have a force of separation as great as that between heaven and the abyss in their fierce urgency — and so he gains rebirth. Because he is pressed by the extreme suffering of hell, the moment he hears the Buddha’s name he calls upon it with his whole mind and strength. Apart from this thought there is absolutely no other thought. Though he has not personally realized single-mindedness, yet his heart is in the end utterly without any other thought.]

The Sutra of Contemplation on the Buddha of Measureless Life tells us that when a person of the five heinous offenses and the ten evil deeds, at the end of life, sees the signs of hell appear, someone teaches him to recite the Buddha; though he only recites ten times, or even fewer than ten times before he breathes his last, he is still able to rely on the Buddha’s compassionate power and be reborn carrying his karma. This is because these ten recitations, compared with ordinary ten recitations, have a force of separation as great as that between heaven and the abyss in their fierce truthfulness — and so he is able to be reborn. Because he is pressed by the extreme suffering of hell, when he hears that reciting the Buddha can keep him from falling into hell and instead be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss, he then recites with his whole mind and strength. Apart from this thought of Buddha-recitation there is absolutely no other thought. Though he has not personally realized single-mindedness, yet at death his heart is in the end completely without any thought other than the thought of Buddha-recitation.

[Five heinous offenses]Five kinds of extreme offenses contrary to principle, namely: killing one’s father, killing one’s mother, killing an arhat, drawing blood from a Buddha’s body, and breaking up the harmonious Sangha. Because these five are extremely evil acts, committing any one of them causes one to fall into the uninterrupted hell. [Ten evil deeds]Namely, killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, idle talk, harsh speech, divisive speech, greed, anger, and folly.
The Collected Writings of Master Yinguang
Preface to the Guide to Pure Karma for Beginners says:

[The minds of sentient beings are like water, and Amitābha Buddha is like the moon. When sentient beings are fully endowed with faith and vows and sincerely move the Buddha, then the Buddha responds to them, as when the water is clear and the moon appears. If the mind is not pure, not sincere, in accord with greed, anger, and delusion, and turned away from the Buddha, then it is like turbid, moving water; though the moon does not withhold its shining upon it, still it cannot clearly reflect its image.]

The minds of sentient beings are like water, and Amitābha Buddha is like the moon. When sentient beings are fully endowed with faith and vows and sincerely move the Buddha, then the Buddha responds to them, as when the water is clear and still and the moon appears (a metaphor for the pure mind of right mindfulness moving Amitābha Buddha to come and receive one). If the mind is not pure, not sincere, in accord with greed, anger, and delusion, and turned away from the Buddha, then it is like turbid, moving water; though the Buddha-moon does not withhold its shining upon it, still it cannot clearly reflect its image (a metaphor for the agitated, turbid, confused mind not being able to move Amitābha Buddha to come and receive one).

blocks.text: The Instruction of Chan Master Yuanxian

inline.s: (The original text is recorded from the Collected Meanings of the Path Within the Path and Again the Path.)

[Chan Master Yuanxian]A monk of the Caodong school of the Ming dynasty (1578–1657). A man of Jianyang (Fujian province), lay surname Cai, style Yongjue. Born on the nineteenth day of the seventh month of the sixth year of Wanli. By nature highly intelligent, in youth he studied the Confucian classics and was quite diligent, being admitted as a student of the county school. In the thirtieth year of Wanli (1602), at the age of twenty-five, he first learned that apart from Zhou and Confucius there was also the learning of the Buddha, and so widely studied the scriptures and treatises, probing deeply into their principle. The following year he took refuge with Huijing of Shouchang, and at forty left home under him. In the forty-sixth year of Wanli (1618), when Shouchang passed away, he served his disciple Yuanlai of Boshan, received the full precepts, and then went to Xianglu Peak, Jinxian Hermitage, Heshan, and other places to study for several years. In the ninth month of the third year of Tianqi (1623), returning to Min, as he passed through Jianjin he heard someone on a boat reciting the Lotus Sutra, and his mind opened in a sudden awakening. In the sixth year of Chongzhen (1633), he received the Yunqi precepts text from Guangyin of Wengu, and the following year dwelt at Gushan in Fuzhou; he then successively dwelt at Kaiyuan Temple in Quanzhou, Zhenji Temple in Hangzhou, Baoshan Temple in Yanzhou, and other monasteries. Later he returned again to Gushan, rebuilt and restored its halls and towers, and greatly revived the ancestral wind of the Dong [Caodong] line, so that people of the time all called him an ancient Buddha reborn. The master’s aspiration was toward the West, and he often urged people to cultivate the pure karma. He passed away on the seventh day of the tenth month of the fourteenth year of Shunzhi of the Qing, aged eighty. His disciples included Daopei of Weilin and many others. His works include the Extensive Record of the Elder Venerable Yongjue, in thirty scrolls; the Brief Commentary on the Surangama Sutra, in ten scrolls; the Brief Commentary on the Diamond Sutra, in one scroll; the Palm [Guide] of the Prajna Heart Sutra, in one scroll; the Approximate Meaning of the Four-Part Precepts, in four scrolls; the Development of the Study of the Precepts, in three scrolls; the Essential Teachings of Pure Compassion, in one scroll; the Textual Research on the Explanatory Comments of the Chan School, in four scrolls; the Sequel to the Transmission of the Lamp Record, in six scrolls; the Record of the Spreading of Interpretations of Jianzhou, in two scrolls; the Inner Collection of Meditative Leisure, in two scrolls; the Outer Collection of Meditative Leisure, in eight scrolls; and other works.
[The merit of pure karma, though accumulated in ordinary days,
and yet the final thought at death is the most crucial
. For whether one is born in the Pure Land or in the defiled world, whether one enters the holy or the ordinary — it is solely this single thought that turns them around.]

The merit of pure karma, though accumulated in ordinary days, it is the final thought at death that is most crucial. This is because whether one is born in the Pure Land or in the defiled world, whether one enters the stream of the holy or the position of the ordinary, is completely determined by this final thought at death!

[I often see people who recite the Buddha, who ordinarily all speak of seeking rebirth in the Pure Land, but when they come to the end of life, most have no right mindfulness. Some, greedy for life and afraid of death, cling to this skin-bag; some, gazing at their wives and children, cannot bear the parting; some, mindful of their family wealth, cannot let it go; some, because circumstances are adverse, end their lives with regret; some, pressed by the suffering of illness, depart in pain. Having lost right mindfulness, they are content to sink and fall.]

I often see people who recite the Buddha, who ordinarily all say they seek rebirth in the Pure Land, but when they come to the end of life, most have no right mindfulness. Some, greedy for life and afraid of death, cling to this physical body; some, watching their wives and children, cannot bear the parting; some, mindful of their family wealth, cannot let it go; some, because circumstances are adverse, end their lives with regret; some, pressed by the suffering of illness, depart in pain. Having lost right mindfulness, they can only sink and fall along with the deluded thoughts of death.

[I urge practitioners who have come to this point simply to believe in truth the words of the scripture, solidify their right mindfulness, let go of all things, and recite the Buddha while awaiting the end. Alas! The matter of the gate of death is great; in an instant comes the next life. A single mistaken thought brings suffering through kalpas — can one not fear this!]

I urge practitioners, when they come to the moment of death, simply to believe in truth the words of the scripture, solidify their right mindfulness, let go of all things, and recite the Buddha without cease, until the breath ends. Alas! The matter of birth and death is great; in an instant comes the next life. If the final thought at death goes wrong, and so one suffers through kalpas — can one not fear this!
